newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish privatisation faces Telekom court hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Turkish privatisation faces Telekom court hurdle.

text.p: Daren Butler

Turkey's ambitious privatisation plans face the major hurdle of a court ruling on Turk Telekom's sell-off next week which could handicap what is a key element in the government's economic programme, market analysts said.

Forecasts of multi-billion dollar revenues from sell-offs in 1997 have been the engine of sustained upward momentum in the share market in recent months and a major factor in plans to balance this year's budget.

These expectations will be put to the test next Tuesday when the constitutional court, acting on a challenge by mainly leftist MPs, rules on the legality of selling the state telecommunications company, analysts said.

"We have to stress that a negative constitutional court decision could endanger all the privatisation projects planned for 1997," Hakan Tezguler, research director at Eczacibasi brokerage said in the economic daily Dunya.

Turk Telekom, slated for sale in the second half of 1997, is the centrepiece of a sell-off programme which has moved sluggishly since its inception 10 years ago, raising total revenues of just $3 billion despite bold government forecasts each year.

State Minister Ufuk Soylemez on Thursday fuelled fresh expectations of accelerated sales, announcing Turkey would prepare at least $750-800 million worth of sell-offs during January, after only $300 million in the whole of 1996.
Governments have failed to fulfil similar forecasts in the past because of legal and parliamentary challenges, including the annulment of a previous draft law on the sale of Turk Telekom.
Concern about the ruling's outcome was voiced on Thursday by a legal adviser to Turkey's privatisation authorities.

"Law number 4161 will be annulled on January 21. You don't need to be a soothsayer (to predict that)," said Yahya Zabunoglu, a legal adviser to the Privatisation Administration (OIB). But he went on to say there was no certainty about the outcome.

Turkey, which expects to raise around $3.5 billion from the sale of Telekom, last month appointed a consortium headed by Goldman Sachs to advise on the sell-off. Analysts believe the sale process is so far advanced that a court ruling will mean only a limited delay in the sale.

The breakneck speed of share market gains in recent days -- 18.1 percent in the Istanbul market index since January 2 -- is testimony to market confidence in the coalition's resolve to follow through with its promises on privatisation.
Some market analysts played down the effect of an annulment next week, pointing to other imminent sell-offs which would cushion any near-term blow to sentiment.

"A negative result has already been discounted and would only have a small impact, but there would be a tremendous impact upwards if there is approval," Volkan Sari, market strategist at leading Istanbul brokerage Global said.

The scheduled privatisation and division of Etibank into three banks, set to be finalised this month, will offset any disappointment over annulment of the Telekom law, he said. Revenues of around $500 million are anticipated from the sale.
In December Turkey accepted leases for the operation of seven Turkish ports over a 30-year period for a total $250 million.
The government is also planning to open tenders in the first quarter for the partial sale of state refiner Tupras and petroleum products distributor Petrol Ofisi.
The Islamist-conservative coalition established last June by Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan sees privatisations as a major weapon in combating Turkey's considerable deficit problems.

Erbakan said on Wednesday the 1996 budget deficit would be 1,200 trillion lira ($10.6 billion), compared with 316.6 trillion a year earlier. Parliament last month approved for 1997 a zero-deficit budget which depends on considerable revenues from privatisations.
($1=112,700 Turkish lira)
